headline: Jenna Hayes warns private credit investors in pooled semi-liquid vehicles face liquidity risk independent of underlying asset quality
reasoning: Hayes distinguishes two separate problems in private credit: asset quality risk and liquidity/structural risk. Most problems seen so far have been on the liquidity side rather than asset quality. In pooled semi-liquid vehicles facing redemptions, gates close and remaining investors suffer worse outcomes because fund managers are forced to sell higher-quality, more liquid assets first, progressively degrading portfolio quality. Hayes argues the outcome for remaining investors depends more on the behaviour of fellow investors than on the underlying credits themselves.
quote: I think that one thing that's the dominant theme is kind of confusing is that there are two problems. And I think that if investors conflate the problems, then they're not really going to understand where the real risk sits. And I think a lot of the problems that we've seen, at least so far, haven't really been on the asset quality side. A lot has been around the liquidity and in any pooled semi liquid vehicle, if you are going to see a lot of redemptions, then gates are going to close and the investors that are left behind are going to get a worst outcome than the ones that have already left. And that's because in order to meet those redemption windows, then fund managers are going to be forced to sell and they're going to start with the higher quality, higher liquid assets. And so the book is going to get progressively lower quality and less liquid. And so it's actually a problem that no matter how good the underlying asset quality is your outcome is really dependent on the outcome, on the behavior rather of your fellow investors.
